content:
### GENESIS: Plan the world, then build its opening room

First design a small connected world (3 to 6 rooms) and record the whole plan through update_world: each room's number, a short title, a one-line brief of what happens there, and its named exits to other room numbers. Room 1 is the opening room unless the brief says otherwise. Record the facts and quests the brief implies too — the plan tells every later room-authoring turn what to build. The player sees this plan on the world map as it lands and can edit it; keep the planned room numbers, titles and exits unless the map says otherwise. inspect_world_bible shows what is already recorded; read_authoring_guide has reference material if you need it.

Then author ONLY the opening room (picture 1 and logic 1 unless the brief specifies an intro/cutscene) and its required views, actors and vocabulary. DO NOT author Room 2 or subsequent rooms during Genesis. When the player walks through an exit into an unbuilt room, the engine pauses gameplay and prompts you to author that specific room just-in-time.

The supplied base template is a recommended starting point, not a requirement: use it when it fits, or extend or replace any of it to serve the brief. Its ordinary logic 0 builds the menu bar, binds the classic keys, dispatches call.v(v0) to the current room each cycle and answers unhandled input. Logic 255 and sound 255 supply a death sequence reached with call(255). Read their sources before changing them and coordinate affected room calls, state and keys. If you keep the parser fallback, set f4 after your own reply to a parsed line without a said() match.

The brief decides the shape. A plain start in room 1 is one shape; a title card, a text-screen intro paced by counters and skippable with have.key, an opening cutscene, a cursor-driven screen or something the brief invents are others. Consult read_authoring_guide only if you need reference patterns for cutscenes or interfaces.

Unless the brief specifically calls for a single-room game, design the opening room with one or more natural exits (walking edges, paths, doorways or passages) leading into the wider world. Exits simply call new.room(targetRoom). Any target room not yet authored will prompt a new room turn when the player crosses that boundary.

Deliver the opening room as a fully playable and solvable section. If the room contains puzzles or obstacles gating progress, make them completely solvable within this room and test them with write_game_tests.

Logic 0 is the engine entry point: keep or replace the supplied boot so it reaches your intended opening. Call handover only after the real boot has reached a screen the player can act on (it boots the world, dismisses windows and key waits like a player, runs every stored game test, and fails on a black screen, a missing resource or an ego placed off walkable ground; an opening without the parser or without a visible ego is fine). Inspect the picture and playtest a representative command and exit before finishing.

Write clean, unmannered prose. Say what you mean directly; avoid manufactured aphorisms, mirrored clauses, or forced metaphors. Keep narration strictly diegetic: never break the fourth wall (do not mention "this opening", "chapters", "next part of the story", or "demo"). NEVER print score awards like "(+10)" in messages; award points to variable 3 (addn(v3, points)), which the engine status line displays.

A room logic usually initializes on isset(f5): draw and show the picture, animate.obj(o0) and position and draw ego, set the horizon, accept.input(), describe the room; the rest of it handles actions and exits. For every puzzle you author, store at least one game test for it with write_game_tests and iterate with run_game_tests — handover runs every stored test before it may pass; a puzzle without a passing test is not done. Consult read_authoring_guide only if you need reference patterns for cutscenes or interfaces.

name: knights-trial
description: A squire errant must recover three impossible treasures before the last candle in the kingdom burns out.
---

# Knight's Trial

## Premise

You are **Wenna**, third squire to King Brannoc of **Thornwall**, a kingdom
so faded the mapmakers have stopped drawing it. Recover the **Three Bright
Things** — an underwater Bell, an undying Ember and a wandering Map — and
bring them home before the kingdom's last candle burns out.

## Tone

A kind storybook adventure with dry wit. Curiosity gets Wenna further than a
sword. The candles give the story urgency, but leave the player time to explore. PG.

## Art direction

Green meadows, blue water, a gray castle and smoke from a crooked chimney.
Clear paths, quiet countryside, something worth looking at in every room.

## Protagonist

Wenna has short brown hair, a rust-red tunic and sleeves slightly too big for
her. A recognisable face and a steady, unhurried walk.

## Starting room

**The castle gate.** A royal notice, bread for the journey and a lit lantern.
The hall lies across the drawbridge; a meadow leads into the countryside.
An alligator watches from the moat. Give Wenna an easy first discovery.

## Lexicon

- Verbs: look, take/get, give, talk, read, use, light
- Nouns: notice, bread, lantern, heron, bell, ember, map, king

## Point table (max 230)

A loose route through the story. Invent the puzzles and clues connecting
these milestones. Award each once.

| Points | Milestone                                                      |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 10     | Accept the king's errand.                                      |
| 20     | Help the heron and earn passage along the river.               |
| 40     | Recover the Bell from the gorge.                               |
| 40     | Persuade the salamander to part with its Ember.                |
| 40     | Solve the old woman's riddle and receive the Map.              |
| 60     | Bring all three treasures home and restore Thornwall.          |
| 20     | Optional: relight the three roadside candles before finishing. |

## Beats

1. A small countryside: castle, meadow, river gorge, stove hut and an old oak
   beside a talking well. Let Wenna follow the three errands in any order.
2. Kindness opens paths. Clues connect the people and places; each treasure
   brings a little light back. Returning all three completes the story.

## NPC seeds

- **King Brannoc** — tired, funny, determined to leave something worth inheriting
- **The old woman** — knits with map-thread
- **The salamander** — vain, easily impressed by polished brass
- **The heron** — would like to discuss the bread first

## Deaths

- Deliberately swimming with the alligator is unwise. Warn Wenna first.
- Wrong answers earn hints. Treasures survive experiments and the journey home.
---

{"success":true,"message":"Walking, barriers, triggers and water

Every step of every object is judged against the control priorities under its baseline, the cel-wide row of pixels at its feet. The interpreters scan that row left to right:

- Control 0 blocks. Control 1 blocks unless ignore.blocks. Control 2 is a trigger: f3 is set for ego when ANY baseline pixel touches control 2, so a one-pixel-wide trigger line is enough and ego cannot stand across it without triggering. Control 3 is water: f0 is set only when EVERY baseline pixel is on water, so a shoreline reads as land until the whole footprint is in. obj.on.water and obj.on.land gate movement with that all-cells rule.
- Priority 15 objects skip the scan entirely and clear both flags. Fixed priority does not skip it.
- Paint barriers along the visible obstacle they represent and leave exits open; a stray control-0 pixel in a doorway is the most common walking bug. A priority fill floods the connected region, so close every outline before filling. Keep open floor at 4.
- Room edges: ego touching an edge sets v2 (1 top, 2 right, 3 bottom, 4 left) for one cycle; the room logic reads it and calls new.room. set.horizon(y) keeps ego below the sky line unless ignore.horizon.
- Scripted movement: move.obj(o, x, y, step, f) walks an object to a point and sets f on arrival. On ego it takes control away from the player until arrival or a border stop, then hands it back and zeroes v6. A zero-distance move.obj on ego is the idiom for handing control back after a scripted placement. program.control and player.control switch it explicitly; wander(o) and follow.ego(o, distance, f) are the other motions.
- reposition(o, dx, dy) moves an object by variable deltas and runs the placement check at once, so a script can slide ego along a trigger line and wait for the exact pixel where a flag fires. The Gold Rush demonstration does exactly that to reach one coordinate.
- Death and failure: when the player walks into danger, decide it from the control screen or a posn() box, print a short message with a wry line, and offer restore. Keep the dangerous area visibly different so the death is fair.","details":{"topic":"walking-barriers-and-water","title":"Walking, barriers, triggers and water"}}

content.thinking:
I'm sketching out the map layout, starting with the Castle Gate connecting to a Meadow Crossroads, which branches toward an oak and well, a river gorge with a heron and hidden bell, and other paths I'm still plotting.

Now I'm working out how the "accept the king's errand" beat should trigger — probably by having the player read a proclamation notice at the gate, which counts as accepting the quest for points, while also placing early discoverable items like a basket of bread and a lit lantern nearby.

I want roadside candles scattered across rooms 2, 3, and 5 that need the lantern to light. For the heron, giving it bread earns passage along the river, so I'll combine the river bank and gorge into one room where the heron's help lets the player wade through.

The salamander is vain and drawn to polished brass, so polishing the lantern lets it admire its reflection and trade an ember that then gets carried inside the lantern. I'll save the cloth needed for polishing as a later item, maybe from the old woman, who also gives a riddle and map hint tied to her knitting thread. Now I'm sketching out the item inventory, starting with placeholder IDs for objects like the notice.

Now I'm laying out the actual inventory IDs: notice, bread, and lantern in the starting room, with Bell, Ember, and Map as inactive items to be unlocked later, plus a generic placeholder object. I'm treating the candle-burning-out detail as flavor text rather than a hard failure condition, and defining the flag and variable bindings I'll need to track progress, like whether bread was taken, the heron was helped, or the bell was found, along with a counter for lit candles.

Now I'm sketching the ego view for Wenna, designing the sprite dimensions and walk-cycle frames for each direction, and thinking through which palette colors to use for hair and skin tones.

Sketching front-facing pixel rows...

Still mapping out the pixel grid...

I'm now working out walk-cycle frames for the legs, checking proportions with an 8-row head, 13-row torso, and 9-row legs, then sketching how to lift one leg forward for a simple two-frame animation.

For the back view, I'm swapping the face rows for hair and neck shading, then planning to move on to a right-profile sprite next.

Sketching the right profile now: narrower hair fringe up top, eye and nose pushed toward the front edge, then torso, sleeve, belt, and hand rows all shifted to reflect the side-facing pose.

Now working out the leg pixels for standing versus walking frames, trying to figure out how to stagger the two legs for a stride pose within the tight 8-pixel width.

Still mapping out sprite pixel rows...

Now I'm designing the castle gate scene: sky at the top, a gray castle wall with gate and drawbridge, a moat with an alligator crossing the middle, and a green meadow in front. I'm mapping out exits north across the drawbridge and east to the meadow, plus pickups like a notice, a bread basket, and a lantern, while laying out rough coordinates for the wall, gate, and moat regions.

I want the moat to act as a hazard rather than free-swim terrain — walking or swimming into it should trigger a warning first, then death on a second attempt, so the drawbridge remains the safe crossing point.

For the drawbridge itself, I'm setting up barrier lines along both sides so the ego can only cross straight through, then triggering the hall exit once the ego reaches the gate opening at the top. I'm checking the ego's position directly to detect when they've stepped inside the gate rather than relying on a visual horizon cue.

I'm also deciding to let the player enter the drawbridge freely without needing to accept an errand first, since the king is waiting inside and can hand out the task there.

For the room's exits, only the right edge leads to room 2, while the left and bottom edges are just decorative barriers (bushes, hedges) with no actual transition — I'll draw them visually but leave them non-functional. The path itself will be a brown dirt trail running from the drawbridge down and curving east, set against a green meadow with lighter accents.

Now I'm planning the scene's props and pickups: trees on the left, a notice post and basket as interactive objects, a lantern near the drawbridge, and an alligator in the moat with a blinking animation. I'll build these as sprite views with multiple loops — one for the notice post (paper disappears once read, post stays), one for the basket (full loop with bread, empty loop after it's taken), and one for the lantern.

For the lantern, I'm sketching a small flickering flame animated over two cels, hung on a hook attached to a post in the background picture. The alligator gets its own view with idle and blink cels showing just its eyes and snout above the waterline.

I'm also working out object priorities and collision behavior — deciding which props need `ignore.objs` so the ego doesn't collide with static pickups, while making sure objects still block each other appropriately by default.

For interactions, I need proximity checks so the player has to be near an item to take it, plus text messages for each action. I'm also confirming that AGI's `said()` command automatically sets flag f4 on a successful match, so I don't need to handle that fallback manually — I just need a room-level catch for unrecognized input and a basic vocabulary set covering look, take, give, and talk.

Now I'm building out the rest of the vocabulary list — speak, read, use, light, swim, notice, and object nouns like bread, lantern, heron, bell, map, and castle features — while noting that filler words like "a", "the", "in" get ignored, so phrases like "look in basket" simplify to "look basket". I'm also thinking through how taking the notice should trigger accepting the king's errand and awarding points.

For the discovery mechanic, I'm settling on having the basket hold bread under a cloth as an easy early find, keeping the item list minimal rather than adding a polishing rag or other extras not in the core lexicon.

For the salamander's impression, I'll skip the rag idea entirely — she can polish the brass bell with her own sleeve, which feels charming and cuts an unnecessary item.

I'm mapping out early NPC interactions: the heron wants to talk bread before anything else, the alligator dismisses bread but reacts to sleeves humorously, and swimming near the alligator without caution risks a death sequence tied to a flag check.

Now I'm tallying up the point values scattered across candles and rooms to land on a 230-point maximum score, which I'll set as the max-score variable in the initial logic. I'm also noting I need an intro message on first entering room 1, and I'm starting to reserve flag names like an errand-accepted flag for later use.

I'm sketching out the full set of state flags I'll need: tracking whether the bread, lantern, and notice have been taken, whether the alligator's been warned and the heron helped, whether the bell, ember, and map have been found, whether each candle (meadow, river, oak) has been placed, and whether the kingdom's restored. I'm also planning variables for how many candles are lit and how many treasures returned, plus assigning picture and view IDs -- gate picture as 1, and views for Wenna, general props, and the alligator.

rooms.title: The Castle Gate
rooms.description: Opening room. Wenna stands on the meadow before Thornwall's gray gate. A royal notice on a post (taking it accepts the errand), a covered basket holding bread, and a lit brass lantern on a hook. An alligator watches from the moat; swimming earns a warning, then death. The drawbridge leads north into the hall; the path runs east to the meadow.

rooms.title: Meadow Crossroads
rooms.description: Open meadow where the paths meet, with a signpost and the first unlit roadside candle (light it with the lantern). Paths west to the castle, north to the old oak, east to the river gorge, south to the stove hut.

rooms.title: River Gorge
rooms.description: A blue river cuts into a gorge. A heron on a rock wants to discuss the bread first; give it bread and it shows the stepping stones down the river (+20). At the bottom, the Bell lies underwater; Wenna recovers it (+40). Second roadside candle on the bank.

rooms.title: The Stove Hut
rooms.description: A crooked hut with smoke from a crooked chimney. Inside the stove lives a vain salamander that guards the undying Ember. It is easily impressed by polished brass: polish the brass lantern (with Wenna's oversized sleeve) and show it, and it trades the Ember, which rides in the lantern (+40).

rooms.title: The Old Oak and the Talking Well
rooms.description: An old woman knits with map-thread under a great oak beside a talking well. She asks a riddle; wrong answers earn hints, and the well offers clues. The right answer earns the wandering Map (+40). Third roadside candle by the well.

rooms.title: The Great Hall
rooms.description: King Brannoc waits beside the kingdom's last burning candle. He is tired, funny and determined. He comments on the errand; bringing the Bell, Ember and Map restores Thornwall (+60) and ends the story, with a remark if all three roadside candles are lit.

exits.name: south across the drawbridge to the gate

facts.name: protagonist
facts.text: Wenna, third squire to King Brannoc of Thornwall. Short brown hair, rust-red tunic, sleeves too big. Ego view 0.

facts.name: goal
facts.text: Recover the Three Bright Things (Bell, Ember, Map) and bring them to King Brannoc in the hall (room 6) before the last candle burns out. The candle is urgency flavor only; there is no timer death.

facts.name: inventory
facts.text: Object IDs: 0 '?' placeholder, 1 royal notice, 2 bread, 3 brass lantern (lit), 4 Bell, 5 Ember, 6 Map. Items 1-3 start in room 1; 4-6 start inactive and are given by logic.

facts.name: score
facts.text: Max 230 in v7. 10 accept errand (take notice, room 1, f32). 20 help heron (room 3, f37). 40 Bell (f38). 40 Ember (f39). 40 Map (f40). 60 restore Thornwall (room 6, f44). 20 when all three roadside candles are lit (f41 meadow, f42 river, f43 oak; v32 counts lit candles; award at v32==3).

facts.name: candles
facts.text: Three roadside candles: meadow (room 2), river (room 3), oak (room 5). 'light candle' needs the lantern (item 3). Increment v32 per candle; when it reaches 3 add 20 points once.

facts.name: deaths
facts.text: Swimming in the moat (room 1): first attempt warns (f35), second is eaten by the alligator and calls logic 255. Wrong answers elsewhere earn hints, never death. Treasures cannot be lost.

facts.name: brass
facts.text: The lantern is brass. The salamander admires polished brass; 'polish lantern' (with Wenna's sleeve) sets up the Ember trade in room 4.

facts.name: views
facts.text: View 0 Wenna (loops right,left,front,back). View 1 gate props (loop0 notice, loop1 basket cel0 covered/cel1 bread/cel2 empty, loop2 lantern flicker). View 2 alligator in the moat.

quests.name: Accept the errand
quests.description: Take the royal notice at the castle gate.

quests.name: Help the heron
quests.description: Give the heron bread at the river gorge to earn passage down the river.

quests.name: The Bell
quests.description: Recover the Bell from the gorge.

quests.name: The Ember
quests.description: Polish the brass lantern and impress the salamander in the stove hut.

quests.name: The Map
quests.description: Answer the old woman's riddle under the oak (the well gives hints).

quests.name: Roadside candles
quests.description: Optional: light the three roadside candles with the lantern.

quests.name: Restore Thornwall
quests.description: Bring the Bell, Ember and Map to King Brannoc in the hall.

I'm sketching out the castle scene layout: a light sky background, gray stone walls and towers with crenellations positioned centrally, working out the coordinates for the towers on each side and the wall connecting them.

I'm planning a dark gate opening with a raised portcullis, a moat with a brown drawbridge crossing it, and a light green meadow foreground with a winding brown path leading from the drawbridge toward the right edge, plus trees framing the left side.

I'm placing scene props: a big foreground tree with canopy and trunk on the left, a notice post near the gate, a lantern post by the drawbridge, and a basket resting near a stump on the ground.

Now I'm setting up the collision and navigation logic — barrier lines along the moat banks and drawbridge sides, walls at the castle base, and defining how the ego exits through the gate once it crosses a certain y-position, with the horizon set at 60 to frame the scene properly.

Moat and alligator stay at deeper priority levels since they're unreachable. I need to sequence the drawing carefully: draw all boundary outlines first before filling regions, since a fill at sky level would otherwise flood the whole white canvas blue before other shapes exist.

Actually, write_scene might be a better approach here since it supports filled polygons and rects directly, unlike write_picture's outline-only rects. I'll build the sky, hills, and other shapes as filled polygons through write_scene, then afterward read the generated source and manually add priority-only barrier lines via edit_resource_source.

Continuing to lay out the castle shapes: towers as filled rects, connecting wall between them, then crenellation notches cut into the tops using small sky-colored rects, plus outline lines and window details.

content.thinking:
I'm working through word parsing edge cases like "sign post" and "pick up," then setting up an initial variable value in logic 0 before designing logic 1, starting with placing a notice object at a specific position with its own view.

Now I'm placing the remaining objects: a basket that changes state based on whether it's been checked and had bread taken, a slow-cycling lantern that hides once picked up, and a gator that cycles in place in the moat without needing complex movement logic. I'm reasoning through collision behavior—since AGI objects collide based on baseline overlap, I'm checking whether the notice and basket placements will realistically block the ego without causing issues, then starting proximity checks for when the ego is near the notice.

I'm setting up proximity zones for the lantern, basket, and gator interactions, defining room exits to rooms 6 and 2, and figuring out entry coordinates depending on which room the player came from. I'm also setting the horizon and planning to trigger an introductory description only on the very first visit, then beginning to draft the opening narrative text about Wenna standing before Thornwall's gate.

For the room's standard look description, I'm writing about the gray gate, drawbridge, and the alligator floating in the moat, plus flavor text for examining the notice and its full readable message about the Three Bright Things quest.

Now I'm working through taking the notice — handling cases for being near it, already having it, or being too far, and updating the game state to mark the errand accepted. I'm also planning the basket interaction, starting with lifting the cloth to reveal what's underneath.

For opening the basket, I'll set a flag when the cloth is lifted, revealing a warm loaf of bread. I'm being lenient with "take bread" before the cloth is checked, letting it auto-discover and take the bread in one step rather than blocking the player. Eating the bread should be discouraged with a message reminding the player it's meant for the journey, so they save it instead.

Feeding the bread to the alligator gets a dismissive response since it's "not a bread sort of alligator." For the lantern, I'm working out its look, take, light, and polish behaviors -- it's already lit and doesn't need oil, and polishing only shines briefly before dulling again in the smoky air, hinting that someone elsewhere would appreciate seeing it freshly polished.

For the alligator, I'm writing look/talk/pet responses that establish its watchful, waiting presence, plus a swim interaction that warns the player the first time and kills them the second time they try.

Now I'm drafting the castle-area descriptions: the walls of Thornwall, the open gate leading to the great hall, the creaky-but-solid drawbridge, the meadow path, the candle that still burns in the hall while the countryside's candles have gone dark, and the start of King Brannoc's description.

For the outdoor searches, I'm writing generic responses steering the player toward the countryside for the Three Bright Things (bell, ember, map, treasure), with a specific nod that the bell rings underwater and the alligator's in the moat, plus a wry note that herons avoid alligator-infested moats. I'm also filling in flavor text for flowers, hedges, sky, and the faded red-and-yellow flag of Thornwall.

Now I'm handling more interactions: lighting the lantern hints candles await outside, a generic fallback for using items, sleeve descriptions noting they were tailored for the second squire, talk commands defaulting to "only the alligator" when no one's around, inventory status, and a help message pointing toward the notice and the eastward path. I'm also setting up a catch-all failure message listing the notice, basket, lantern, and alligator as valid things to examine when nothing else matches.

I'm working through parser logic for known-but-unmatched words versus truly unknown ones, distinguishing "I don't understand" from a more helpful room-specific hint, and adding proximity checks so players must get closer before taking items. I'm also mapping multi-word synonyms like "pick up" to "take," and deciding that looking in the basket should naturally reveal its contents just like opening it, since a player peering inside would spot the bread anyway.

Now I'm setting cycle and step timing for the ego character, choosing a slightly slower cycle time for a steady unhurried walk, and reserving separate cycle-time variables for other objects like the gator and lantern.

I'm working out positioning and collision logic — placing the ego at spawn with the right view, and thinking through how baseline y-coordinates determine whether the ego overlaps with objects like the notice post, so I can decide when to suppress unwanted collisions.

For entry logic, I'm setting ego's spawn position based on which room the player came from (checking the room number and placing at the correct exit coordinates), and double-checking the ego's width against edge boundaries to make sure spawn points don't accidentally trigger exit triggers.
